title: The Ethics Hotline
theme: Running a school ethics reporting system and navigating moral complexity
description: You run your school's ethics reporting system. Over 10 cases — from copied homework to teacher misconduct — you'll face genuine moral dilemmas where doing the right thing isn't always clear. Every decision shapes the school's trust in the system.
learning_objectives: Understand the complexity of ethical decisions when multiple values conflict
Practice balancing confidentiality, fairness, and courage
Learn to evaluate evidence before making judgments
how_to_play: Each round presents an ethics case reported to you. Read carefully, consider all perspectives, and choose how to handle it. There are rarely perfect answers — the goal is thoughtful reasoning.

glossary_terms.definition: Keeping information private that was shared with you in trust
A person who reports wrongdoing, often at personal risk
Following fair steps before making a judgment — hearing all sides, gathering evidence
An unfair preference for or against something, often unconscious
Being answerable for your actions and their consequences

rounds.title: The Copied Homework
rounds.situation: Your first case arrives, {player_name}. A Class 8 student reports that his classmate, Neha, copied his entire science assignment word-for-word and submitted it first. The teacher gave Neha full marks and accused the original writer of copying. He has his rough drafts as proof. Neha is the class topper and teacher's favourite.
rounds.story: The reporting system is new. How you handle the first case sets the tone for everything.
rounds.image_prompt: Two Indian school assignment papers side by side, one clearly copied, student looking upset in background
rounds.coaching_moment: The first case you handle defines whether people believe the system works or is just for show.

choices.label: Present the evidence to the teacher
choices.description: Take the rough drafts to the science teacher and let the evidence speak. Ask them to reconsider.
choices.consequence_hint: The teacher might correct the grades, or they might get defensive about favouring Neha

events.description: The teacher looks uncomfortable but agrees to review the rough drafts. Neha is called in.

choices.label: Talk to Neha privately first
choices.description: Give Neha a chance to come clean before escalating. Maybe she'll confess and fix it herself.
choices.consequence_hint: This protects Neha's dignity but risks her denying it or destroying evidence

events.description: Neha turns pale. She says, 'I was under so much pressure. My parents expect perfect grades.'

choices.label: Escalate to the principal directly
choices.description: This involves a teacher's grading error and student copying. It's too big for you to handle alone.
choices.consequence_hint: The principal will handle it officially, but the teacher may resent the system for going over their head

events.description: The principal launches a formal review. The science teacher is visibly annoyed.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Cyberbullying Screenshot
rounds.situation: An anonymous report arrives with screenshots, {player_name}. A group of Class 10 students created a fake Instagram account mocking a classmate, Farhan, using his photos with cruel captions. Farhan doesn't know about the account yet. The screenshots show the creators' real accounts in a group chat.
rounds.story: You have proof of who did it. But acting on anonymous evidence is tricky.
rounds.image_prompt: Phone screen showing mean Instagram posts with a student's photos, anonymous report note beside it
rounds.coaching_moment: Having evidence doesn't automatically make the next step obvious — how you use evidence matters as much as having it.

choices.label: Report to the school cyberbullying team
choices.description: Hand over the screenshots to the designated teacher. Let the official system handle it.
choices.consequence_hint: The official route is thorough but slow — and Farhan might find out about the account before action is taken

events.description: The cyberbullying team calls the students in. The account is taken down within 48 hours.

choices.label: Warn Farhan first
choices.description: Tell Farhan about the account so he's not blindsided. He deserves to know what's happening about him.
choices.consequence_hint: Farhan is warned but might confront the bullies directly, escalating the situation before adults can intervene

events.description: Farhan is devastated but grateful you told him. He wants to confront the group himself.

choices.label: Confront the creators directly
choices.description: Show them the screenshots privately. Tell them to take down the account in 24 hours or you go to the school.
choices.consequence_hint: Fast and direct, but you're acting as judge — and they might turn on the anonymous reporter or on you

events.description: Two of the three students look ashamed. The third says, 'You can't prove anything.' The account stays up.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Teacher Favouritism
rounds.situation: Five students from Class 9 file a report, {player_name}. Their maths teacher, Mr. Gupta, consistently gives higher internal marks to students who attend his private tuition classes. Students who don't attend — including some who score well in exams — get lower internals. They have comparison data across two terms.
rounds.story: This is a systemic issue involving a teacher's income. The stakes just got higher.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian students showing marks comparison sheet to student ethics leader, concerned expressions, school corridor
rounds.coaching_moment: When a complaint involves someone more powerful than you, the system's credibility depends entirely on whether you still act.

choices.label: Document everything and go to the principal
choices.description: Compile the data professionally and present it to the principal as a pattern, not an accusation.
choices.consequence_hint: The principal may investigate, but Mr. Gupta could face no consequences if the school protects him

events.description: The principal reviews the data quietly. Mr. Gupta is called for a 'routine review.' He looks shaken.

choices.label: Advise students to talk to Mr. Gupta first
choices.description: Suggest the students have a respectful conversation with Mr. Gupta about their concern before escalating.
choices.consequence_hint: Gives the teacher a chance to change, but students confronting a teacher about corruption takes enormous courage

events.description: The students look scared. One says, 'He'll just give us even lower marks if we complain.'

choices.label: Gather more evidence first
choices.description: Ask the students to collect one more term's data and get statements from other affected students. Build an airtight case.
choices.consequence_hint: More evidence means a stronger case, but the students suffer another term of unfair grading while you wait

events.description: The students agree reluctantly. One drops out of the complaint, saying, 'It's not worth the risk.'

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Leaked Exam Paper
rounds.situation: Two days before the Class 10 mid-terms, {player_name}, a student slips a note under your door: 'The Hindi paper has been leaked. Some students in 10-B have it. Check with Rohit Menon.' You don't know who left the note. Rohit Menon is the student council secretary — someone you work with every day.
rounds.story: An anonymous tip about someone you know. The exam is in 48 hours.
rounds.image_prompt: Anonymous note on desk, exam papers in background, Indian school student looking shocked
rounds.coaching_moment: When the accused person is someone you trust, the temptation to dismiss the complaint is natural — but justice requires investigating anyway.

choices.label: Go straight to the exam controller
choices.description: This is too serious to investigate yourself. Report it immediately to the teacher in charge of exams.
choices.consequence_hint: The exam might be changed in time, but Rohit could be falsely accused if the tip is wrong

events.description: The exam controller changes the paper overnight. The school investigates 10-B.

choices.label: Talk to Rohit privately first
choices.description: Ask Rohit directly: 'I heard something. Is there any truth to it?' Give him a chance to explain.
choices.consequence_hint: If Rohit is guilty, you're warning him and giving him time to hide evidence. If innocent, you're being fair.

events.description: Rohit goes pale. He says, 'Someone sent it to me. I didn't ask for it. I swear.' You don't know what to believe.

choices.label: Investigate quietly yourself
choices.description: Before reporting, check if 10-B students actually have the paper. Ask around discreetly.
choices.consequence_hint: You verify the claim, but the exam is in 48 hours and every hour of delay increases the damage

events.description: Within an hour, a friend from 10-B confirms: 'Yeah, some kids have it. It's on a WhatsApp group.'

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Stolen Money
rounds.situation: {player_name}, a Class 7 student, Aditi, reports that ₹500 disappeared from her bag during lunch. She suspects Kiran, the boy who sits next to her, because he was the only one in the classroom. But she has no proof — just suspicion. Kiran's family is known to struggle financially. Aditi's parents are threatening to call the police.
rounds.story: Suspicion without proof. Poverty and theft are dangerously linked in people's minds. What do you do?
rounds.image_prompt: Indian school classroom, empty school bag open on desk, young student looking worried, another student looking scared
rounds.coaching_moment: The most dangerous ethical mistake is assuming someone is guilty because of who they are rather than what they did.
rounds.timer_narrative: Aditi's parents are coming to school in an hour...

choices.label: Investigate without naming Kiran
choices.description: Ask the class teacher to check CCTV (if available) and ask all students who were in the classroom. Don't single out Kiran.
choices.consequence_hint: Fair process that protects Kiran from false accusation, but slower and Aditi's parents want immediate action

events.description: CCTV shows three students entered the classroom during lunch. Kiran was one, but so were two others.

choices.label: Question Kiran directly
choices.description: Pull Kiran aside and ask him directly, but kindly. Give him a chance to return the money without consequences.
choices.consequence_hint: If he took it, this gives him an out. If he didn't, you've just accused a kid based on his economic status.

events.description: Kiran starts crying. 'Everyone always blames me because we're poor. I didn't take it.'

choices.label: Ask Aditi to be sure before acting
choices.description: Tell Aditi that accusation without proof can hurt an innocent person. Ask if she's checked her bag thoroughly and other possibilities.
choices.consequence_hint: This is careful and fair, but Aditi might feel you're not taking her complaint seriously

events.description: Aditi rechecks her bag. The ₹500 is in a zippered pocket she forgot about. She feels terrible.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The False Accusation Aftermath
rounds.situation: The stolen money case resolved, but word got around. {player_name}, Kiran's mother comes to school in tears: 'My son hasn't eaten lunch for three days. He says everyone thinks he's a thief.' Meanwhile, Aditi's parents are demanding the school install cameras in every classroom. How do you address the damage?
rounds.story: Even when you handle things carefully, people still get hurt. The question is what you do about it.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian mother wiping tears in school office, young boy looking down, student leader sitting across, empathetic atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: Justice isn't just about getting the right answer — it's about repairing the harm caused along the way.
rounds.timer_narrative: Kiran's mother is waiting for a response...

choices.label: Advocate publicly for Kiran
choices.description: Make a statement in the class that the investigation found no evidence against anyone. Ask students to stop rumours.
choices.consequence_hint: This clears Kiran's name publicly but draws more attention to the incident

events.description: The class listens. A few students apologize to Kiran privately. His mother calls the school to say thank you.

choices.label: Work quietly behind the scenes
choices.description: Ask the class teacher to pair Kiran with supportive students. Get Aditi to privately apologize.
choices.consequence_hint: Less dramatic but more targeted — helps Kiran without making him the centre of attention again

events.description: Aditi writes Kiran a note: 'I'm sorry I suspected you.' Kiran starts eating lunch again.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Repairing Trust After the Money Case
rounds.situation: The stolen money situation got messy, {player_name}. Kiran was questioned directly and the whole class knows. Even though the money was found in Aditi's bag, students whisper about Kiran. His attendance has dropped. A teacher says, 'You shouldn't have handled it that way.' Two more students have pulled their reports from the ethics system, saying they don't trust it.
rounds.story: Your approach damaged trust — both in Kiran and in the system. Now you need to rebuild.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student leader looking at empty ethics complaint box, worried expression, school notice board in background
rounds.coaching_moment: Mistakes in ethics work aren't fatal — but only if you acknowledge them and change your approach.
rounds.timer_narrative: The principal wants to discuss whether to continue the ethics system...

choices.label: Own the mistake publicly
choices.description: Write a note to the school acknowledging that the process was flawed and announcing stronger safeguards going forward.
choices.consequence_hint: Brave and transparent, but admitting a mistake publicly is hard and some will use it against you

events.description: Students are surprised by the honesty. Two students re-submit their reports. A teacher says, 'That took guts.'

choices.label: Quietly improve the process
choices.description: Add new rules: no student will be questioned without evidence; all cases require a teacher mediator present.
choices.consequence_hint: Better systems prevent future harm, but the current damage to Kiran and to trust remains unaddressed

events.description: The new rules are posted on the notice board. Some students notice. Most don't.

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The Discrimination Report
rounds.situation: {player_name}, a Muslim student, Zara, reports that during a group activity, a classmate said: 'You people are always like this.' The teacher heard it and said nothing. Zara says this isn't the first time — similar comments happen regularly and teachers ignore them. She wants something done but is terrified of being labelled 'too sensitive.'
rounds.story: Discrimination complaints are the hardest to handle because they challenge the culture itself.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian Muslim girl student looking hurt but determined, filing a written complaint, school ethics office
rounds.coaching_moment: When someone reports discrimination, the first question to ask yourself is not 'Was it that bad?' but 'How many times has this happened before they finally spoke up?'
rounds.timer_narrative: Zara needs to know you'll act before she loses the courage to follow through...

choices.label: Take it to the principal with Zara's consent
choices.description: Explain to Zara that this needs adult intervention. If she agrees, present her case formally.
choices.consequence_hint: Official action sends a strong message, but Zara will become visible and may face social consequences

events.description: The principal takes it seriously. A school-wide sensitization session is announced. The teacher involved looks uncomfortable.

choices.label: Address it at classroom level first
choices.description: Talk to the class about respectful language without naming Zara. Address the specific comment as an example of what's not acceptable.
choices.consequence_hint: Protects Zara's anonymity, but a classroom talk may feel too mild for a systemic problem

events.description: The class listens. The student who made the comment doesn't realize it's about them. Zara is safe but unsure if things will change.

choices.label: Support Zara to speak up herself
choices.description: Coach Zara to address the classmate directly — with you present for support. Empower her to own her voice.
choices.consequence_hint: Empowering, but puts the burden on the victim and requires enormous courage from a student already hurting

events.description: Zara speaks up during the next class. Her hands shake, but her words are clear. The classmate is stunned into silence.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Plagiarism by Your Friend
rounds.situation: Your close friend Arjun confides in you, {player_name}: 'I copied my entire English essay from the internet. I know it's wrong but I had no time — my parents are fighting at home and I couldn't concentrate.' He's not reporting it. He's telling you as a friend. But you run the ethics system.
rounds.story: When your role and your friendship collide, which one wins?
rounds.image_prompt: Two Indian students talking privately in school library, one looking guilty, the other looking conflicted
rounds.coaching_moment: The hardest ethical dilemmas aren't between right and wrong — they're between two things you care about deeply.

choices.label: Convince Arjun to come clean
choices.description: Tell him, 'I can't report you as a friend. But you need to tell the teacher yourself. I'll go with you if you want.'
choices.consequence_hint: This preserves the friendship and gives Arjun agency, but he might not follow through

events.description: Arjun hesitates but agrees. You walk with him to the English teacher's office. He tells the truth.

choices.label: Keep it between friends
choices.description: This was told in confidence, not reported to the ethics system. As a friend, you'll help him rewrite it tonight.
choices.consequence_hint: You protect Arjun and the friendship, but you're compromising the ethics role you hold

events.description: You stay up until midnight helping Arjun write an original essay. He submits it. No one knows.

choices.label: Report it to the teacher
choices.description: Your ethics role requires it. Tell the English teacher what Arjun told you, even knowing it will hurt the friendship.
choices.consequence_hint: Principled and consistent, but Arjun trusted you as a friend and you betrayed that trust

events.description: The teacher calls Arjun in. He stares at you in the corridor: 'I told you as a friend.' He doesn't speak to you for a month.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Teacher Misconduct Report
rounds.situation: A Class 11 student, Meera, files a report that a teacher, Mr. Saxena, makes inappropriate personal comments — calling her 'beautiful' in front of the class, asking her to stay back for 'extra help' alone. {player_name}, Meera says she's scared and wants you to handle it without her name being used. Two other girls say similar things happened to them.
rounds.story: This is the most serious report you've received. It involves adult misconduct against minors.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian girl students looking worried, filing report in ethics office, serious and tense atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: When the accused person has power over the complainant, protecting the complainant comes first — always.
rounds.timer_narrative: Meera has to attend Mr. Saxena's class tomorrow...

choices.label: Go directly to the principal — now
choices.description: This is beyond your role. Tell the principal immediately, share all three accounts, and ask that Meera and the others be protected.
choices.consequence_hint: The principal should handle this, but some principals protect teachers over students. You're trusting the system.

events.description: The principal is shocked. An immediate investigation is ordered. Mr. Saxena is removed from Meera's class pending inquiry.

choices.label: Help the students write to the school management
choices.description: If the principal might not act, help the students write a joint letter to the school management committee with documented incidents.
choices.consequence_hint: Bypass the principal — more powerful, but slower and the students are exposed while waiting for action

events.description: The management committee receives the letter. An emergency meeting is called for this week.

choices.label: Tell a trusted female teacher
choices.description: Find a senior female teacher the students trust and ask her to take this forward. She'll know the right channels.
choices.consequence_hint: Smart — an adult ally with institutional knowledge can navigate this better than you, and the students feel safer

events.description: Mrs. Verma, the senior-most female teacher, is furious. She goes straight to the principal with the students' accounts and doesn't leave until action is confirmed.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Whistleblower Protection
rounds.situation: It's the end of the school year. {player_name}, the ethics system has handled 23 cases. Most went well. But one student who filed a report against a popular senior is now being socially isolated — no one sits with them at lunch, they've been dropped from the cricket team. They come to you: 'I wish I'd never filed that report. The system punished me for doing the right thing.'
rounds.story: The hardest question: Does the system protect the people brave enough to use it?
rounds.image_prompt: Lonely Indian student sitting alone at lunch table, other students in groups in background, student leader approaching
rounds.coaching_moment: A reporting system that doesn't protect its reporters is worse than no system at all — it punishes courage.
rounds.timer_narrative: The student is considering transferring schools...

choices.label: Create a formal protection policy
choices.description: Write to the principal proposing an anti-retaliation policy. Document what happened to this student as the reason it's needed.
choices.consequence_hint: A policy sets the foundation for future protection, but this student needs help right now, not next year

events.description: The principal approves a whistleblower protection clause. It's the first of its kind in the school's history.

choices.label: Rally support for the student personally
choices.description: Use your position to publicly stand with this student. Eat lunch with them. Get others to do the same. Show that filing a report doesn't make you an outcast.
choices.consequence_hint: Visible solidarity sends a powerful message, but you're using your social capital — some might turn against you too

events.description: You sit with them at lunch on Monday. By Wednesday, three more students join. The cricket captain quietly re-invites them to practice.

choices.label: Both — act now and build for the future
choices.description: Support the student personally today while simultaneously proposing the protection policy for all future reporters.
choices.consequence_hint: The most complete response, but it requires enormous energy and commitment in your last weeks as ethics head

events.description: You write the policy on Monday and sit with the student at lunch on Tuesday. By the end of the week, three teachers email you: 'This is the best thing the ethics system has done.'

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

coaching_moment: Ethics isn't about having all the right answers — it's about caring enough to ask the hard questions and having the courage to act on them.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: The Ethics Hotline Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of The Ethics Hotline. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
